newsitem.title: JAPAN: SUMO-WOMEN MAKE DECIDEDLY LIGHTWEIGHT, FEMININE DEBUT.
newsitem.headline: SUMO-WOMEN MAKE DECIDEDLY LIGHTWEIGHT, FEMININE DEBUT.

text.p: For all its archetypal heavyweight maleness, the modern debut of women's sumo wrestling in Japan on Sunday was a decidedly lightweight, feminine affair.

Much of the traditional ceremony of male sumo was missing at the inaugural tournament organised by the newly formed Japan New Sumo Federation and there was a ban on such unladylike techniques as throat-slapping and head-to-head charges at the face-off.
But even so, the women still cheered the 500 spectators with the popular chalk-throwing, thigh-slapping warm-up routines which preceded the 15 bouts, some of which lasted just a few seconds.
The main difference to the male competition, though, came on the scales. The heaviest competitor weighed in at a mere 135 kgs, about half the bulk of the present heaviest male sumo wrestler.
The lightest was a mere 48 kgs, a laughable size in men's events.

And, unlike the bare-chested men who are renowned for bulging bellies, the leotard-dressed women on display in Osaka, showed no signs of training for their bouts on a traditional diet of beer drinking and huge meals.
"The image of martial art sports is changing completely," said Keiko Fukui, one of the curious 500 at the ground-breaking tournament in the office building basement.
"Look at the pink leotards they are wearing. I wouldn't mind if my daughter said she wanted to do this," she said.
In sumo wrestling, two contestants basically meet head on in a charge and then use their weight and skill to make the other fall to the ground.
Unlike the men, though, where there are no weight divisions, the women's competition copied the example of boxing and Greco-Roman wrestling by using different weight categories.

Women's sumo wrestling did exist in Japan from the 19th century to the start of World War Two but it was simply an entertainment featuring naked ladies, not a sport. It then went out of vogue and disappeared -- until now.

Kimio Kobashi, chairman of the Japan New Sumo Federation, said there were about 70 registered women wrestlers. This was just the first of a number of tournaments which will feature a national championships later in the year.

Most women are athletes in other sports such as judo which is another contrast to their male counterparts who, in following a 1,300 year tradition, are among the most respected and highest paid sports stars in Japan.
But, surprisingly, there was no disdain from Yutaka Matsumura, a representative of the fiercely conservative Sumo Federation which runs the sport.
"Japan's traditional sumo, with its history of 1,300 years, has changed dramatically over the years and will continue changing," he said..
Yoshiki Fuse, a sumo coach, who now trains women, said female competitors had adapted well to the sport.
"Most of the girls in my club were previously judo wrestlers. They are all used to most of the (sumo wrestling) stuff I teach," he said.
An amateur male sumo wrestler who was at the event agreed there was nothing wrong with women taking up the sport.
"If the Sumo Federation is supporting it, why not? It shouldn't be limited to the men if women are also willing," he said.
Another male spectator, Takeshi Yamamoto, said: "It makes me realise how Japanese women have got stronger. They play soccer, rugby, and now they even do wrestling."
But he sounded a note of traditional propriety: "When it comes to sumo, I guess it's okay only because they are wearing what they are wearing and not naked like the male players."
One competitor, Sanae Kikuchi, who weighed in at a trim 53 kgs, ), said she was wary of making the sacrifices her male counterparts make in deliberately putting on weight to improve their power.
"If they said I had to get fat, I'll have to give it up," she said.
